title: Singapore Minister Defends SIA's Air India Stake as $1.5B Funding Request Stirs Scrutiny
excerpt: Singapore Airlines' 25.1% stake in Air India faces political backlash in the city-state as the Indian carrier seeks $1.5 billion in fresh equity after a record $2.33 billion annual loss.
body:
• Air India is seeking about $1.5 billion in fresh equity from owners Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines after posting a record $2.33 billion annual loss.
  • The request has triggered political scrutiny in Singapore, where opposition lawmakers questioned the exposure of state investor Temasek, which majority-owns Singapore Airlines.
  • Singapore's transport minister told parliament the investment decision belongs to Singapore Airlines' board and Singaporeans are not paying for it.
  • Discussions are ongoing with no decision taken; the airline wants the funds immediately, likely in tranches, as a multi-year turnaround continues.

Singapore's transport minister on Tuesday defended Singapore Airlines' investment in Air India after the Indian carrier's request for about $1.5 billion in fresh equity from its owners sparked a political backlash in the city-state, pulling the struggling airline's turnaround into a debate over Singapore's national reserves.

Responding to questions in parliament, Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow said investment decisions belonged to Singapore Airlines' board and that Singaporeans were not paying for the Air India investment. "Whether its specific investment in Air India proves valuable is for (Singapore Airlines) and its shareholders to answer," he said, adding that the airline had not sought further capital from shareholders.

Context and Background

Reuters reported last month that Air India had approached Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines about equity funding, months after the carrier and its budget arm Air India Express posted a combined record annual loss of $2.33 billion for the fiscal year ended March — more than double the prior year's losses. Two people familiar with the matter told Reuters the carrier wants the funds immediately, though the infusion is likely to happen in tranches, and that Singapore Airlines would need to contribute its share of the proposed infusion for it to go through.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=awWIEtJNvDc

It would be one of Air India's largest publicly reported requests for shareholder funding since Tata took control of the former state-owned carrier in 2022. Singapore Airlines holds a 25.1% stake in Air India and has booked its share of the Indian carrier's losses, weighing on its own earnings. Air India and Tata Sons have not commented publicly on the funding request; Singapore Airlines said it was working closely with Tata Sons to support Air India's transformation programme but declined to comment on the airline's finances.

The airline has also been hit by Pakistan's airspace ban on Indian carriers, disruptions to its international network from the conflict involving Iran, and the fallout from a 2025 crash that killed 260 people.

Political Scrutiny in Singapore

The funding request drew a sharp reaction from Workers' Party lawmaker Kenneth Tiong, who argued in a social media post that because Singapore Airlines owns about 25% of Air India and state investor Temasek in turn owns most of the Singapore carrier, the request was "not only a question for private shareholders." Temasek owns and manages its own assets, and its reserves form part of Singapore's national reserves.

"I will not support, nor expect, any future use of Temasek's funds to prop up Air India via Singapore Airlines. If Singapore Airlines wants to continue its bet on Air India, it should do so on its own two feet, and not on Temasek's."

— Kenneth Tiong, Workers' Party member of parliament

Tiong filed a parliamentary question asking whether losses from Singapore Airlines' foreign associates have been assessed against its capacity to provide essential transport services. A government minister also said the funding report had prompted anti-Indian abuse online and asked police to examine the comments.

Siow told parliament the flag carrier was a listed company that funds investments from its own balance sheet, and that its ability to serve Singaporeans was not adversely affected. Singapore Airlines said in a statement that investments in India have been and will continue to be funded through its internal resources, subject to board approval and a disciplined capital allocation framework, calling the investment a long-term strategic commitment aligned with its multi-hub strategy.

Impact and Analysis

The dispute lays bare the financial strain of Air India's multi-billion-dollar revamp. Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran has said the turnaround could take up to a decade, and the carrier's losses have widened even as it refurbishes its existing fleet and rebuilds its network.

For Singapore Airlines, the episode tests the limits of its overseas expansion strategy. The carrier has argued it must grow abroad because there is a limit to how many people will fly to or from Singapore — a point Siow repeated in parliament — but booking Air India's mounting losses has made the India bet a political liability at home.

Diaspora Angle

Air India remains the primary carrier connecting the Indian diaspora to India on many long-haul routes, and its turnaround matters directly to millions of passengers who fly it for holidays, family visits, and business. The outcome of the funding request will shape how quickly the airline can complete fleet refurbishment and stabilize operations — the two complaints that surface most often from overseas Indian travelers.

What's Next

Discussions between Air India, Tata Sons, and Singapore Airlines are ongoing, and no decision has been taken, the sources told Reuters. Any infusion would require board-level sign-off on both sides. For Singapore Airlines, Tuesday's parliamentary defense buys the board room to maneuver — but the next time Air India needs cash, the political cost of writing the cheque will likely be higher.
